title: The manjis, deeper
hookLine: his network of teachers, women and men, spread the sangat far

cards: A low wooden frame with rope woven across it, the household cot or seat of Punjabi courtyards. Nothing grand. Sit on it under a tree, and people can gather on the ground around you.
Sikh tradition says that's the picture behind a word from Guru Amar Das's time: manji. He lived at Goindval, and the sangat kept growing in places far from his door.
So, tradition says, he appointed teachers, women and men, to sit on a manji in their own region and hold the sangat together there.

teach.b: We've met the manjis before on this path, as a story. Today, look at the idea. First, a manji was a plain household seat, not a throne.
The teacher sat close to the people, near enough to hear their questions. The authority came from the Guru's teaching, not from the furniture.

Second, it moved the center outward. Instead of everyone traveling to one place, the sangat could meet near home. The Guru's Word, the langar's open row, the hymns: all of it could happen in a village courtyard.
Third, tradition remembers women among these teachers; the Guru's network trusted them to lead. Accounts differ on the details. The heart of the telling is that the sangat spread far.
And what was a manji meant to hold? Guru Nanak had already given the measure, in Sri Rag, paraphrased: how is the true sangat known?

teach.h: WHERE THE ONE NAME IS SPOKEN.
teach.b: Where the One Name is spoken.
That's the test. Not the size of the crowd, not the fame of the teacher, but whether the Name is spoken there.
A Sikh who explains a hymn to a child, or invites a coworker to langar, does in a small way what the manjis did: carries the sangat a little further from the center, and sits close enough to listen.

how: Sikhs remember the manji system in histories of Guru Amar Das and in katha; today local gurdwaras and their sangats carry on the work of gathering people near home around the Guru's Word.

games.q: the sangat is growing in places far from Goindval. you're the Guru. what do you do?
o: appoint teachers, women and men, to hold the sangat near home.
stop people from joining until you can visit.
games.why: tradition says Guru Amar Das set up manjis: teachers in each region, sitting close to the people.

practice: Let one thing you've learned on this path come back, man too jot saroop hai, by any door, not the pyre, and choose the one you could say most simply.

Picture one person who might like to hear it, a child, a friend, a parent, and see yourself beside them, saying it in plain words and listening to what they ask. If you pray, Waheguru can ride each breath out.

wordCard.voice: The manjis. In Sikh tradition, the seats of teachers, women and men, who held the sangat together far from the Guru's town, wherever the Name was spoken. Today's word.

orig.note: a small rope seat or cot; in Sikh tradition, the seat of a teacher in Guru Amar Das's network.

carryVoice: Your line: spread it far. A plain seat and a listening ear can carry a long way. Until tomorrow.
